data.cultural_impact: The name Hirad carries a deep significance in Islamic culture as it signifies being a guide and providing direction in life. This name is particularly special because knowledge is highly valued in Islam, and the one who imparts knowledge and wisdom acts as a Hirad for others. Moreover, Hirad is also associated with the Prophet Muhammad, who is considered the perfect guide for humanity. Thus, a person named Hirad carries this noble title with a profound sense of honor and responsibility to lead others towards the right path.
data.spiritual_significance: On a spiritual level, the name Hirad signifies being a source of spiritual enlightenment and guidance. It implies that the individual named Hirad is meant to act as a bridge between Allah and His creation. By embodying the qualities of guidance and wisdom, Hirad can help others on their journey towards Allah and lead them to seek spiritual growth and development. This name also holds a powerful reminder to the bearer that they must remain true to their purpose and continue to seek knowledge and wisdom throughout their life, as Hirads have a profound impact on the lives of those around them.

historical_references.reference:
Ibn Al-Athir in his 'Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh' records that during the reign of the Abbasid Caliph Al-Qadir Billah (r. 1031-1045 AD), a man named Hirad bin Mas'ud Al-Jazari was a prominent figure in Baghdad, famous for his inventions, including the programmable hydraulic organ.
Context: During the Abbasid Caliphate, Baghdad was a center of scientific and cultural progress. This period saw the flourishing of various fields of knowledge, including mathematics, astronomy, and engineering.

Al-Qifti in his 'Kitab Al-Fihrist' mentions Hirad as a prominent musician and poet in the court of the Umayyad Caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik (r. 724-743 AD). He was known for his beautiful singing voice and his poetry that extolled the virtues of the caliph.
Context: The Umayyad Dynasty ruled the Islamic world from Damascus during this period. The court of the caliph was the center of artistic and literary activities, and musicians and poets were highly respected figures.
